approaches.name: Medial minimally invasive approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Short medial distal incision with epiperiosteal plate tunneling from distal to proximal beneath intact soft tissue

sources.title: Minimally Invasive Approach To The Distal Tibia
MIPPO versus interlocking nail fixation for adult extra-articular distal tibial fractures
MIPPO versus ORIF for distal tibial fractures in adults: meta-analysis

procedure_applications.condition: An extra-articular or simple minimally displaced articular fracture is amenable to indirect reduction and bridge plating

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the medial ankle accessible and uninterrupted AP, lateral, and mortise fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Confirm indirect reduction is feasible, template plate length and screw sites, and mark the saphenous structures and fracture extent before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the medial malleolar tip, medial tibial border, ankle joint, greater saphenous vein, and planned proximal screw sites.

incision.text: Make a 3-5 cm straight or gently curved medial distal incision ending at the medial-malleolar tip, with separate proximal stab incisions for diaphyseal screws.

superficial_interval.text: Carry dissection directly through subcutaneous fat, identify the saphenous vein and nerve, and hold them anteriorly with a blunt retractor.

deep_interval.text: Preserve periosteum and advance the blunt plate tip proximally in the epiperiosteal plane beneath intact soft tissue.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous saphenous plane, intact periosteum, epiperiosteal tunnel, then medial distal tibia.

structures_encountered.text: Greater saphenous vein, saphenous nerve, medial periosteum, medial malleolus, and distal tibia are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Saphenous vein and nerve, medial skin, periosteal blood supply, tibialis-posterior region, and joint with distal screws are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep the tunneler and plate on bone in the epiperiosteal plane and visualize/protect the saphenous structures at distal and percutaneous screw sites.

retraction_hazards.text: Use blunt anterior retraction of saphenous structures and avoid forceful subcutaneous tunneling that perforates skin or strips periosteum.

exposure.text: Permits medial bridge-plate insertion while preserving the metaphyseal soft-tissue envelope and fracture blood supply.

limitations.text: Does not directly expose comminuted articular reduction and may allow malalignment if indirect reduction is not rigorously controlled.

extensions.text: Add a small medial arthrotomy for medial-malleolar cartilage assessment or a separate fragment-specific incision when indirect reduction is inadequate.

indications.text: Use for extra-articular distal-tibia fractures and simple minimally displaced complete-articular patterns reducible by ligamentotaxis, forceps, or percutaneous lag screws.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose direct articular exposure for displaced comminuted plafond injury and an anterolateral tunnel when medial soft tissue is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Insert a precontoured medial plate distal-to-proximal, verify plate-to-bone position, and place proximal screws through targeted stab incisions.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use serial AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique images to control length, rotation, coronal/sagittal alignment, plate position, and joint-safe screws.

closure.text: Confirm hemostasis and saphenous-structure freedom, then close each small incision without tension over prominent hardware.

complications.text: Complications include malalignment, saphenous neuritis, wound problems, infection, hardware irritation, delayed union/nonunion, and screw penetration.

bailouts.text: Convert to a limited direct reduction window when length or alignment cannot be restored indirectly rather than locking a malreduction beneath the plate.

questions.question: Which structures are held anteriorly?
questions.answer: The greater saphenous vein and saphenous nerve.

questions.question: What is the central biologic goal?
questions.answer: Preserve metaphyseal soft tissue and blood supply by avoiding fracture exposure.

approaches.name: Infrapatellar tibial nail entry approach
approaches.corridor: Midline infrapatellar exposure through a tendon split or medial/lateral paratendinous interval to the anterior tibial plateau entry point

sources.title: Nailing Limited Open Approach To The Distal Tibia
Infrapatellar Approach For Intramedullary Nailing Of The Tibial Shaft
Review of proximal tibia entry points for intramedullary nailing
Suprapatellar versus infrapatellar tibial nailing: systematic review and meta-analysis

procedure_applications.condition: A tibial fracture is treated with a traditional infrapatellar intramedullary nail entry
A distal fracture is nail-compatible and alignment can be maintained with the knee flexed

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with knee flexed enough for infrapatellar entry and unobstructed AP/lateral imaging from knee through ankle.

setup.text: Review nail-specific entry guidance, plan reduction aids for distal alignment, and ensure guidewire and protection sleeves match the selected nail system.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark inferior pole of patella, patellar tendon borders, tibial tubercle, joint line, and tibial shaft axis.

incision.text: Make a longitudinal midline incision from the inferior patella toward the tibial tubercle, centered on patellar tendon.

superficial_interval.text: Split patellar tendon centrally or open fascia along its medial or lateral border and retract tendon without violating the knee joint.

deep_interval.text: Release retropatellar fat pad from anterior tibia and move it posteriorly to reach the anterior plateau while keeping menisci and capsule intact.

layers.text: Skin, tendon or paratendinous fascia, retropatellar fat pad, anterior proximal-tibial cortex, then medullary canal.

structures_encountered.text: Patellar tendon, retropatellar fat pad, anterior tibial plateau, tibial spines, meniscal margins, and medullary canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Patellar tendon, menisci, articular cartilage, posterior proximal-tibial cortex, and anterior cortex during reaming are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Confirm the guidewire in both planes before opening cortex; keep it centered over canal on AP and immediately anterior to articular margin without breaching posterior cortex on lateral.

retraction_hazards.text: Protect patellar tendon with a sleeve or retractor and avoid forceful tendon displacement or unrecognized intra-articular passage.

exposure.text: Provides direct extra-articular access to the proximal tibial entry site for guidewire, entry reamer, and nail insertion.

limitations.text: Knee flexion can make maintenance and fluoroscopic assessment of proximal or distal fracture alignment more difficult than semi-extended techniques.

extensions.text: Choose a paratendinous interval instead of tendon split when appropriate; change to a semi-extended entry strategy if alignment cannot be controlled safely.

indications.text: Use for tibial intramedullary nailing when a traditional flexed-knee infrapatellar entry permits accurate reduction and entry trajectory.

relative_contraindications.text: Consider suprapatellar or lateral-parapatellar semi-extended entry when flexion worsens alignment or standard access is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Follow the selected nail's entry recommendation; an overly distal or anterior start risks anterior cortical damage while a posterior trajectory risks posterior-cortex penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm entry wire and opening device in true AP and lateral views before canal entry, then monitor reduction and nail trajectory through distal segment.

closure.text: Irrigate entry tract, repair a tendon split or paratendinous fascia anatomically, and close without tendon tethering.

complications.text: Complications include anterior knee pain, patellar-tendon injury, malalignment, cartilage or meniscal injury, cortical breach, infection, nonunion, and hardware symptoms.

bailouts.text: Withdraw and redirect an inaccurate entry wire before opening cortex; change positioning or approach if acceptable canal trajectory cannot be obtained.

questions.question: Where is the AP entry point?
questions.answer: On the anterior plateau, just medial to the lateral tibial spine and centered over the canal.

questions.question: What must be avoided on the lateral view?
questions.answer: Posterior-cortex penetration and an excessively anterior/distal start.

questions.question: What are the tendon options?
questions.answer: Midline transtendinous split or medial/lateral paratendinous exposure.

approaches.name: Posterolateral approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Between peroneal tendons/muscle laterally and flexor hallucis longus medially, with a separate superficial plane to fibula

sources.title: Posterolateral Limited Open Approach To The Distal Tibia
A systematic review of posterior pilon fractures
Strategies for surgical approaches in ORIF of pilon fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A posterior or posterolateral plafond fragment requires direct reduction and buttress fixation
Posterior malleolus and fibula can be treated through one posterolateral incision

positioning.text: Position prone or lateral with posterior ankle accessible and fluoroscopy configured before prepping.

setup.text: Map posterior fragments and peroneal vascular anatomy on CT, decide whether fibula is fixed first, and plan any separate anterior or medial window.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark Achilles lateral border, posteromedial fibular border, fibular tip, sural-nerve course, and posterior ankle joint.

incision.text: Incise along posteromedial fibular border from fibular tip proximally as required, never medial to the lateral Achilles border.

superficial_interval.text: Raise full-thickness flaps, identify sural nerve under superficial fascia and retain it in lateral flap; for fibula, open peroneal fascia and retract peroneals medially.

deep_interval.text: For tibia retract peroneals laterally, develop interval between peroneals and FHL, incise FHL lateral border, and retract FHL medially to protect posteromedial bundle.

layers.text: Skin, sural-nerve plane, peroneal fascia, peroneal-FHL interval, posterior tibial periosteum, then posterior plafond.

structures_encountered.text: Sural nerve, peroneal muscles/tendons, FHL, fibula, peroneal vessels, posterior tibia, and posterior tibiofibular ligament are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Sural nerve, peroneal artery/vein or branches, posteromedial neurovascular bundle, peroneal tendons, FHL, fragment blood supply, and cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Stay lateral to FHL when developing tibial exposure, anticipate peroneal vessels, and deflate tourniquet before deep closure to verify hemostasis.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract FHL medially as protection for the posterior tibial bundle and avoid sustained traction on sural nerve or peroneal vessels.

exposure.text: Provides direct posterior-plafond buttress access and permits fibular fixation through a separate plane in the same incision.

limitations.text: Anterior/anteromedial fragments may require a separate incision and direct central articular visualization can remain limited.

extensions.text: Extend proximally on either side of sural nerve or add a separate medial/anterior window after posterior provisional stabilization.

indications.text: Use for posterior-predominant pilon patterns, posterior malleolar fragments, combined tibia-fibula fixation, or compromised anterior skin.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose another fragment-directed corridor when pathology is predominantly anterior/medial or prone/lateral positioning is unsafe.

implant_implications.text: Supports posterior tibial buttress plating and fibular fixation; sequence implants to preserve reduction access and avoid tendon/neurovascular impingement.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Configure AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique imaging in prone/lateral position before incision and verify posterior plate and screw containment.

closure.text: Release tourniquet for deep hemostasis, restore FHL/peroneal intervals and fascia, leave sural nerve untethered, and close full-thickness flaps without tension.

complications.text: Complications include sural neuropathy, peroneal-vessel injury or hematoma, wound breakdown, infection, tendon irritation, malreduction, nonunion, and arthritis.

bailouts.text: Add a separate fragment-specific window when central or anterior reduction cannot be confirmed rather than stripping through the posterior interval.

questions.question: What is the deep tibial interval?
questions.answer: Between peroneals laterally and FHL medially.

questions.question: Which muscle protects the posteromedial bundle?
Which nerve lies in the superficial flap?
questions.answer: The sural nerve, usually retained in the lateral flap.

approaches.name: Posteromedial approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Fragment-directed interval among tibia, posterior tibial tendon, FDL, and FHL with direct protection of posterior tibial neurovascular bundle

sources.title: Posteromedial Approach To The Distal Tibia
A systematic review of posterior pilon fractures

procedure_applications.condition: Posteromedial and posterior plafond fragments require direct reduction and buttress fixation
A posteromedial posterior-malleolus fragment requires direct access

positioning.text: Position prone or in a stable lateral/supine variant that permits direct posteromedial access and planned fluoroscopic views.

setup.text: Use CT to select the safest tendon interval for the dominant fragment and plan neurovascular-bundle handling, posterior plate position, and any second incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark posteromedial tibial border, Achilles tendon, medial malleolus, posterior tibial tendon path, and posterior tibial pulse.

incision.text: Center incision at ankle between Achilles and posteromedial tibial border, continue proximally parallel to tibia and distally along posterior-tibial-tendon course.

superficial_interval.text: Open subcutaneous tissue and fascia to identify the deep fascial layer over posterior tibial tendon, FDL, neurovascular bundle, and FHL.

deep_interval.text: Select interval between tibia and posterior tibial tendon, between posterior tibial tendon and FDL, or between FDL and FHL; the last requires full direct bundle exposure and protection.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous fascia, flexor retinacular/deep fascia, selected tendon interval, posterior tibial periosteum, then posteromedial plafond.

structures_encountered.text: Posterior tibial tendon, FDL, FHL, posterior tibial artery/veins and tibial nerve, posterior capsule, and posteromedial tibia are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Posterior tibial neurovascular bundle, posterior tibial tendon blood supply, FDL/FHL, saphenous structures with medial extension, fragment blood supply, and cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not strip distal posterior tibial tendon from tibia; expose and control the neurovascular bundle directly before using the FDL-FHL interval.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the bundle only under direct view with broad protection and avoid focal pressure or traction on posterior tibial tendon and tibial nerve.

exposure.text: Provides direct reduction and posterior buttress access to posterior and medial fragments and can support medial-malleolar fixation through a full-thickness anteromedial flap.

limitations.text: The interval is anatomy-dense, far posterolateral and anterior fragments may be inaccessible, and tendon/bundle mobilization limits extension.

extensions.text: Create a full-thickness anteromedial flap for medial malleolus or add a separate posterolateral/anterior window for fragments outside the selected corridor.

indications.text: Use for posteromedial pilon, posterior-malleolar, and medial-fragment patterns requiring direct posterior buttress fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose posterolateral or anterior exposure when dominant fragments lie outside the posteromedial corridor or the medial soft-tissue envelope is unsafe.

implant_implications.text: Supports direct posterior buttress plate placement; select an interval and plate position that avoid posterior tibial tendon and neurovascular impingement.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Preconfigure AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique views for the chosen position and verify posterior reduction, plate location, and screw containment.

closure.text: Confirm bundle perfusion and hemostasis, restore each tendon to a free-gliding bed, repair fascia without constriction, and close full-thickness skin tension free.

complications.text: Complications include tibial neuropathy, posterior tibial vascular injury, tendon adhesions or irritation, wound breakdown, infection, malreduction, nonunion, and arthritis.

bailouts.text: Change to a safer adjacent tendon interval or add a second incision when direct bundle mobilization would be excessive or the fragment cannot be controlled.

questions.question: What are the three deep intervals?
questions.answer: Tibia-posterior tibial tendon, posterior tibial tendon-FDL, or FDL-FHL.

questions.question: Which interval mandates direct bundle exposure?
What fixation principle does this approach enable?
questions.answer: Direct posterior buttress plating of posterior fragments.
